planting.note: Bred specifically for heat tolerance, this F1 komatsuna can be sown from spring through the hottest part of summer; give it afternoon shade in July and August to slow bolting and keep leaves tender.

directions: Summer Fest is a Japanese F1 hybrid mustard spinach bred to resist bolting through the heat of summer, when most other Asian greens fail. Sow seed directly and thin as needed; leaves can be cut at baby-salad size in about three weeks or left to size up into full bunching plants within five to six weeks. Its glossy, rounded leaves have the mild mustard-spinach flavor typical of komatsuna, and afternoon shade during peak summer heat further extends the harvest window before the plants eventually bolt.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or, for the sweetest leaves, in late summer for an autumn crop; light frost improves flavor by reducing the mustard-like bite.

directions: Torasan is a Japanese F1 komatsuna prized for dark, glossy, spoon-shaped leaves and a sturdy, upright habit that holds up well to cutting. It grows quickly from direct-sown seed and tolerates both cool spring conditions and light autumn frost, which sweetens the leaves and mellows their mustard-spinach bite. Because it bolts readily once days lengthen and warm, gardeners in hotter regions do best sowing it in a partly shaded bed or as a fall crop rather than pushing it through summer.

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed slightly in spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; give it partial shade in warm-summer regions to delay bolting.

directions: Prize Choy is an open-pollinated pac choi tracing back to Alf Christianson Seed Company breeding from an era when major companies still maintained open-pollinated Asian brassica lines. It forms vase-shaped, 15-18 inch plants with celery-like white stems and tender, glossy green leaves, and is notably uniform and slow to bolt for an open-pollinated type. Grow it as a substitute for napa cabbage in stir-fries and soups, harvesting whole heads at full size or picking outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again baby crop.

planting.note: Sow in early spring or late summer for fall harvest; this semi-dwarf type is unusually tolerant of heat, cold, and rain swings, making it forgiving for shoulder-season plantings.

directions: Ching Chiang is a semi-dwarf Taiwanese bok choy with smooth, medium-green leaves and pale green petioles, bred to reach usable baby-bok-choy size quickly while still holding quality if left to mature further. It shrugs off the weather swings of shoulder-season planting better than many bok choy types, tolerating both a late cold snap and an early warm spell without much bolting or damage. Harvest whole plants at about five inches tall for the most tender baby heads, or let them grow another week or two for a larger stir-fry-sized crop.

planting.note: Direct sow every couple of weeks from early spring through fall for a continuous supply; a bit of afternoon shade in summer keeps the leaves from turning fibrous and bitter before bolting.

directions: This cress was bred by Oregon seedsman Frank Morton as a cross between 'Persian' and 'Curly' garden cress, combining the deeply savoyed, ruffled leaf texture of curly types with a sturdier, more upright habit that lifts leaves clear of soil splash for cleaner cutting. It germinates and grows fast enough to be treated almost like a microgreen, ready for its first cutting in under three weeks, and is notably slower to bolt than most other cress selections, giving several extra cuttings per sowing. Use it as a peppery, tangy addition to salad mixes, sandwiches, and garnishes wherever a sharper bite than lettuce is wanted.

planting.note: Start indoors and transplant out in late summer for a fall harvest; in mild-winter climates it also works as an overwintering crop when set out in early fall for winter and early-spring cutting.

directions: Natacha is a French-bred escarole selected for large, heavy heads packed with abundant, tender leaves surrounding a creamy, well-blanched heart. It stands out for its strong resistance to bolting, tipburn, and bottom rot, which lets it hold in the garden longer than many older escarole types, especially in hot or humid weather. As with other broad-leaved endives, gathering and tying the outer leaves a week or two before harvest deepens the self-blanching of the heart and mellows the characteristic mild bitterness.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring once the soil has warmed a little, or again in late summer for a fall crop; this quick, petite frisee type resists bolting better than larger endive types, so it tolerates a bit of afternoon shade well.

directions: Tres Fine Maraichere, sometimes sold as the Olesh strain, is an old French heirloom frisee endive valued for its petite size and quick growth compared to standard curly endives. Its narrow, deeply cut outer leaves curl into a naturally self-blanching rosette around a tender, creamy heart, and tying the outer leaves closed about a week before harvest whitens the center further. It can be cut young as a frilly, mildly bitter baby green for salad mixes or allowed to fill out into a full head, and it attracts relatively few pests along the way.
